transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Smith. I came in because, well, I can’t seem to stop launching projects lately. 

It just gets to be... a lot. I'll start drafting massive work plans, mapping out all these new certification schedules, completely upgrading my home network... even sending out messages to old contacts I haven't talked to in years. It gets so intense that I just blow past normal limits. Honestly, I don't really slow down until my wife or my director at work has to step in and pull me back.
Have these periods of intense activity ever caused you to be hospitalized or forced you to take a leave of absence from your job?

I haven't been hospitalized, no. But... yeah, I was forced to take a leave of absence. There was a big system migration at work that ended up failing, and they put me on leave right after that. 

It really just kind of affects everything. At home, my wife has had to step in a lot, mainly to manage my spending or to try and stop me from working so late into the night. And a lot of times, just regular conversations with her end up turning into arguments. 

I’ve also pulled away from the things I usually do outside of work—like playing music at church, rock climbing, and a mentoring program I was part of. I just... I realized I can’t reliably show up or follow through with any of it right now.
During these periods of intense activity, have you ever experienced things that others couldn't see or hear, or held beliefs that others found to be clearly untrue?

Yeah, actually. Um... during those really driven stretches, you know, when I was barely sleeping and just pushing all those huge project plans... I did start experiencing things like that. 

Like, I would hear actual comments or voices coming from the background noise of the servers at work. And... I was also reading into my emails and work messages, convinced there were hidden threats in them. So, yeah, that has happened.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a period of intense goal-directed activity, reduced need for sleep, and functional impairment (forced leave of absence, interpersonal conflict) consistent with a manic episode. Crucially, the presence of auditory hallucinations (voices in server noise) and paranoid delusions (hidden threats in emails) during this state confirms the presence of psychotic features, meeting criteria for Bipolar I disorder, current episode manic with psychotic features.

increased social and occupational activity leading to functional impairment
excessive involvement in activities with high potential for painful consequences (spending issues, work failure)
